identity.title: Position: There are futures that benchmark-driven AI cannot see

problem.claim: The paper examines how AI research can preserve discoveries that are initially uncompetitive under benchmark-centered selection.

gap.claim: The authors argue that dominant benchmark-based selection leaves ideas that do not fit its rule without a way to persist, limiting exaptation.

contributions.claim: Argues that benchmark-centered selection in AI taxes exaptation, especially for alignment, interpretability, and safety questions whose needed discoveries may be unforeseeable.
Proposes plural evaluation regimes, protected venues for non-comparable work, long-horizon funding, and training norms that encourage questioning selection rules.

narrative_sequence.summary: Breakthroughs may arise from ideas that cannot be predicted in advance; biological exaptation illustrates how capabilities can become decisive beyond their original function.
Scientific progress depends on allowing ideas to survive periods when current metrics make them appear uncompetitive.
The paper argues that benchmark-centered AI selection taxes this exaptive capacity, with sharper consequences for aligned, interpretable, and safe intelligence.
It recommends several mechanisms for restoring exaptive capacity while retaining benchmarking.

source_observation.claim: The paper connects a broad selection regime to a specific downstream risk: ideas outside the dominant metric may have nowhere to persist, even when future discoveries cannot be specified.

lessons.interpretation: Framing institutional design as a condition for preserving discovery pathways can make a position argument more concrete.
lessons.application: When arguing that an evaluation regime creates blind spots, map the selection rule to the kinds of ideas or research trajectories it prevents from persisting.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the work concerns a narrowly defined task with an agreed evaluation target and no claim about open-ended discovery.

unknowns: The abstract provides no empirical assessment of the proposed mechanisms, nor details about implementation or trade-offs.
It does not specify how plural regimes or protected venues would be evaluated.
